title: Trusting God and Living Wisely
overview: A father urges his son to trust God, value wisdom above wealth, and treat neighbors fairly, promising that this way of life leads to peace.

parts.label: Words to keep close (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: A father figure urges his son to hold on to his teaching, promising a long and peaceful life. Wearing love and faithfulness like a necklace and writing them on the heart means letting loyalty and kindness show on the outside and steer you on the inside.

parts.label: Trust beyond yourself (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: Many readers treat these lines as the core of the chapter: rely fully on the LORD rather than on your own cleverness alone, and he will make your way clear and level. Respect for God and turning from evil are pictured as good for the whole body, right down to the bones.

parts.label: Giving first, accepting correction (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The firstfruits were the first part of each harvest, given to God at the place of worship to show that the whole harvest came from him. The writer admits hard times come too, and frames them as a loving father's correction, words later quoted in the New Testament book of Hebrews.

parts.label: Wisdom worth more than gold (vv. 13-20)
parts.note: Wisdom is pictured as a woman holding long life in one hand and wealth and honor in the other, worth more than any treasure. She is called a tree of life, an image from the garden story in Genesis, and she is the same wisdom God used to set up the earth, the sky and the deep waters.

parts.label: Safe by day and night (vv. 21-26)
parts.note: Keeping good judgment in view is promised to bring steady steps and untroubled sleep. When sudden disaster strikes, the LORD himself is pictured as your security, keeping your foot from being caught like an animal in a trap.

parts.label: Treating neighbors right (vv. 27-35)
parts.note: Pay what you owe and help when you can without stalling, never scheme against or pick fights with people who trust you, and do not envy violent people or copy them. The closing lines say God curses the home of the wicked and mocks the scornful but draws the upright close and favors the humble, and that the wise gain honor while fools get shame.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises of long life, health and wealth here are firm guarantees for the faithful or general patterns of how life usually goes.
think: When have you trusted your own judgment and been glad you did, and when have you wished you had looked beyond it?
